draft.title: Overviews, topic sentences and conclusions
card: It comes first and tells readers what is coming. It gets readers ready for the ideas that follow.
It opens a paragraph and states the main idea of that paragraph. The other sentences in the paragraph then give details that support it.
It comes last and draws the ideas together. It reminds readers of the main points and does not start a new one.
Read together, the overview, topic sentences and conclusion give a text a clear path from start to finish.
draft.remember: Overview: what is coming. Topic sentence: the paragraph's main idea. Conclusion: ideas drawn together.

a.q: A paragraph in a text opens with a topic sentence. What does that sentence do?
opts: It states the main idea of the paragraph
It sums up the whole text for the reader
It tells readers what the whole text will cover
It adds a new idea at the end of the text
a.why: A topic sentence opens a paragraph and names its main idea, so the other sentences can support it. Telling readers what the whole text covers is the job of an overview, not a topic sentence.
a.clue: Think about what one paragraph is mostly about.

b.q: Ravi writes a text arguing that his town needs a skate park. One paragraph covers safety and one covers exercise. Which sentence would suit his conclusion best?
opts: A skate park would keep young people safe and active
A skate park could also bring tourists to our town
This text will explain why our town needs a skate park
Last year, ten students were hurt skating on roads
b.why: This sentence draws together Ravi's two main points, safety and exercise, which is what a conclusion does. The sentence about tourists is tempting because it supports his argument, but it starts a new point, and a conclusion does not do that.
b.clue: Which sentence looks back over points Ravi has already made?

a.best: It states the main idea of the paragraph

b.best: A skate park would keep young people safe and active
